Despite being a product of that deservedly hated, racist midget, Spike Lee, this movie has enough going for it to merit checking out, if only as a time capsule-like glimpse of two eras distinct from our own. I'm convinced that Lee's movies very occasionally become successes in spite of him rather than due to his efforts. Such is the case with Summer of Sam. If this film had been released today I'm sure it would be a media darling. It is a study in just the kind of degeneracy that is at the heart of our current day culture wars.

It's interesting to note which groups have crossed over from the left to the right since both the era of the film (late 70s) and when the film was made (1999). Are we on the wrong side of history? Are today's trannies and antifacists the misunderstood punks of the 70s? ("Nazi Punks Fuck Off" anyone?) Lee couldn't have predicted Trump's America or Clown World, yet can still recognize many of the familiar players who face off in Brooklyn while a killer is on the loose.

It's fairly apparent that Lee was trying to recapture the lightning in a bottle of Do The Right Thing. Frenzied montages are especially reminiscent of that earlier, superior work, as are his attempts at pitting different ethnicities against one another. The stereotyped caricatures can be laughable even when some of their accuracy is undeniable. To Lee's credit he does show that the riots were instigated by blacks and latinos, but whether or not this is simply a token gesture is debatable. Italian Americans can rightly take exception to Lee's portrayal, but equally maligned are the other various subcultures of gays, transvestites, sexualities across the entire spectrum, strippers, punk-rockers, drug-users and drug-dealers, among others. It's a very bleak picture of the time and space to say the least. It's hard to not conclude that Lee is telling us that the eponymous David Berkowitz was God's wrath made manifest to punish New York City's sins.

The acting is fantastic, Leguizamo and Sorvino especially. Even Adrien Brody does well as a character who is very much a fish out of water. A pre-Sopranos Michael Imperioli makes an amusing appearance as the effeminate manager of a gay strip club. That Fran Drescher was excluded from the cast had to have been a scandal. Any fans of disco will love the soundtrack as well, since much of the time the movie feels like Saturday Night Fever meets Silence of the Lambs.

The car ride home scene with Leguizamo and Sorvino is rightly singled out as the gem of the film. Never has the disgusted fallout from a couple's lamented agreement to sexual experimentation been so deftly portrayed. All the emotions are written there on their faces before they even say a word. Sorvino is herself a Jersey girl, so perhaps this role was simply made for her, but I'll admit to having not yet seen Mighty Aphrodite.

Probably the biggest compliment I can pay the movie is that it avoided making any tidy conclusions to bring its stories to a close. The main characters are all fictional and in this case it's fitting that we don't see what becomes of them. Even the court drama that came with Berkowitz' prosecution is omitted so that Google will need to be responsible for everyone knowing that as of 2019 the Son of Sam is still incarcerated after killing six and wounding seven on his deranged killing spree.
